title: Matsya Defended and Prince Uttara
body:
Matsya Defended and Prince Uttara

The violent and mysterious end of Kichaka struck terror into the hearts of the citizens of Matsya, who suspected that Sairandhri was protected by terrible Gandharvas who would not hesitate to destroy the kingdom. Consequently, Duryodhana's spies, who had spent months searching in vain for the Pandavas, began to suspect that Bhima was the mysterious Gandharva who had slain Kichaka and that Sairandhri was Draupadi. Armed with this suspicion, Duryodhana and King Susharma of Trigarta devised a double-pronged invasion of Matsya to unmask the Pandavas before the stipulated thirteen-year period terminated.
King Susharma launched a violent attack on Matsya from the south, seizing the royal cattle and laying waste to the southern provinces. King Virata marched out to oppose them, accompanied by Kanka, Valala, Granthika, and Tantripala, who volunteered to ride chariots to defend their host. A fierce battle ensued in the south. Susharma captured King Virata, throwing the Matsya forces into a state of panic. At Yudhishthira's command, Bhima charged the Trigarta forces, crushed Susharma's vanguard, and rescued Virata from captivity, demonstrating the profound virtue of gratitude (Kritagnata) by risking their lives to protect the king who had given them shelter.
Simultaneously, the main Kaurava army, led by Bhishma, Drona, Kripa, Karna, and Duryodhana, launched a massive surprise attack from the north, despoiling the royal cattle ranches and rounding up tens of thousands of cows. With the king and the veteran army away in the south, the city was left completely unprotected. The young and boastful Prince Uttara, seeking to impress the ladies of the court, loudly declared that he would defeat the Kauravas single-handed if only he could find an expert charioteer to drive his horses.
Sairandhri immediately intervened, suggesting that Brihannala had once been Arjuna's personal charioteer. Reluctantly, Prince Uttara accepted, and as they rode towards the northern front, a massive cloud of dust heralded the approaching Kaurava host. When Uttara beheld the formidable warriors—Bhishma's standard of the palm tree, Drona's ascetic bowl, and Karna's radiant armour—his courage collapsed entirely. He cast away his bow and arrows, jumped from his chariot, and began to flee back towards the city in panic. Arjuna pursued the running prince, dragged him back to the chariot by force, and promised to fight the Kauravas himself if Uttara would only hold the reins and guide the horses.
